title: Knocking Into Things on the Left

patient.name: Mr Ng Cheng Watt
patient.presenting_complaint: Bumps into objects and people on his left side since a recent stroke

history.hpc: Mr Ng had a stroke two months ago and since then keeps bumping into things on his left. He says: 'After my stroke, I keep knocking into things on my left side, the wife say I don't see that side.' He cannot sit still long enough for a full automated field test today. The OT must perform a confrontation visual field test as a gross assessment of his field.
history.pmhx: Recent ischaemic stroke. Hypertension, atrial fibrillation.
history.social_hx: Lives with wife who accompanies him. Uses a walking stick.

examination_findings.fundus: For doctor; field loss here is likely neurological (post-stroke) rather than ocular

investigations.confrontation_visual_field: Confrontation visual field test performed: examiner faces the patient, each eye tested separately, comparing the patient's field with the examiner's using finger/hand movements in each quadrant. The patient consistently misses targets on the left side in both eyes, suggesting a left homonymous field defect (hemianopia) consistent with his stroke. Documented per eye.

diagnosis: A left homonymous visual field defect detected on confrontation testing, consistent with a post-stroke (neurological) cause rather than an eye disease. Confrontation fields are a useful gross test when a patient cannot do formal automated perimetry. The OT competency is correct technique, recognising the pattern, and documenting/escalating; formal fields and diagnosis are the doctor's.

immediate: Recognise that a patient unable to do automated perimetry can still have a useful confrontation field test
Perform confrontation fields correctly: face the patient, test each eye separately, compare quadrants with finger/hand movements
Identify that targets are consistently missed on the left in both eyes (homonymous pattern)
Document the findings per eye and note the likely neurological cause given the stroke history
Flag the field defect to the doctor and suggest formal fields (e.g., GVF) if the patient can cooperate later
Advise on safety given the field loss (fall/collision risk)
follow_up: Doctor to review and arrange formal visual field testing (e.g., GVF for poorly cooperative patients) if needed
Liaise with the stroke/neurology team as appropriate
Reinforce safety strategies for the field loss
patient_education: Explain in simple terms that the test shows he is missing the left side of his vision
Explain this is likely related to the stroke and the doctor will review it
Advise scanning his head/eyes to the left and taking care to reduce bumping/falls
Encourage attending with his wife and using his walking stick

key_points: Establishes the left-sided bumping since the stroke
Recognises he cannot complete automated perimetry today
Notes the stroke and relevant systemic history (AF, anticoagulant)
Confirms he is accompanied and uses a walking aid
Performs confrontation fields correctly, testing each eye separately
Compares the patient's field with the examiner's across quadrants
Identifies the consistent left-sided defect in both eyes
Recognises a homonymous (same-side) defect suggests a neurological cause
Links the field loss to the recent stroke rather than an eye disease
Understands confrontation fields are a gross test when formal perimetry is not possible
Knows formal fields/diagnosis are the doctor's role
Documents the confrontation field findings and likely cause
Flags the defect to the doctor and suggests formal fields if feasible later
Advises on safety given the field loss
Explains the finding to the patient in simple terms
